warmup.q: A program running in a terminal window stops, and the terminal prints Killed. Asked how the program ended, the shell (the program that reads your commands) answers 137. What does 137 tell you?
options: The program found a problem and chose to end with the code 137
Something ended the program with signal 9, the stop no program can refuse, and 137 is 128 + 9
The program ran out of memory for its objects and gave up
warmup.why: When a signal ends a program, the shell reports 128 plus the signal's number. A signal is a short numbered notice the kernel delivers to a process, and number 9, SIGKILL, is the one no program can catch: the kernel ends the program without asking it. So 137 means somebody sent SIGKILL. Often the time allowed for a polite stop ran out, or the kernel itself ended a program that used too much memory. That last case makes the third option tempting. But a Java program that runs out of room for its objects throws an OutOfMemoryError, and if nothing catches it, the program ends with status 1. Nobody chooses 137 on purpose.

sections.h: The kernel's record of a running program: what a process is
sections.html:
Every program on a computer starts the same way: something else starts it. You type ls into a shell, the program that reads your commands, and a moment later ls is running and listing files. While it runs, the kernel, the core of the operating system that runs every program, has to keep notes about it. Which memory is its own? Which files has it open? Who started it? Is it running right now, or waiting? And when it ends, how did it end? Without those notes, the kernel couldn't stop one program from reading another's memory, and it couldn't tell the shell whether ls worked.

A running program plus the kernel's notes about it is a process. Linux keeps the notes in a structure called task_struct, a bundle of fields much like a Java object, one per process. Each process gets a number, its PID (process ID). It also records the PID of the process that started it, its parent, as its PPID (parent process ID). Every process except the very first was started by another one, so processes form a tree with PID 1 at the root.

Unix, the operating system from the 1970s whose design Linux follows, chose family words for all of this, and they fit better than you'd expect. A process has a parent and children. A child whose parent dies is an orphan, and gets adopted. One word is grimmer than the rest, and we'll meet it in the third section.

You can read the notes without special tools. Linux shows them as files in a folder, /proc/<pid>/, one folder per process. Here is head, a program that prints the first lines of a file, reading its own status file in the lab box. (The lab box is the small Linux computer, run by Docker on your laptop, that this track's Try its use.)

Name:	head
State:	R (running)
Tgid:	12
Pid:	12
PPid:	1

PPid: 1 means the box's shell, PID 1, started head. (Tgid, the thread group ID, is about threads, separate lines of work inside one program. The next lesson, Threads, and how the JVM maps them to the OS, explains it.)

The state says what the process is doing at this moment. ps, the program that lists processes, shows it as one letter in its STAT column:

  • R: running, or ready to run as soon as a processor is free
  • S: asleep until something happens, such as a timer, data from the network or a child ending
  • D: asleep in a way that can't be interrupted, usually waiting for a disk
  • T: stopped, paused by someone
  • Z: a zombie, dead and waiting for its parent (the third section explains)

Every process takes the same path through its life, and this lesson walks it in order. A parent creates it (fork). It loads the program it should run (exec). It ends (exit). Its parent collects how it ended (wait). While it lives, other processes can send it signals, short numbered notices such as "please stop". Picture a table in the kernel with one row per process, each row moving through create, run, end and collect. Next, we'll watch one row make the whole trip.

try.title: Read a process's record
steps: From the labs folder, start the lab box: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box.
Run the commands below. The & starts sleep 100, a program that waits for 100 seconds, in the background, so the shell gives you the prompt back at once. $! holds the PID of that background program.
Before the grep line, predict the state of a process that is running sleep 100.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: head -9 /proc/self/status ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd sleep 100 & grep -E '^(State|PPid)' /proc/$!/status kill $!

try.expect:
PIDs will differ:

Name:	head
Umask:	0022
State:	R (running)
Tgid:	12
Ngid:	0
Pid:	12
PPid:	1
TracerPid:	0
Uid:	0	0	0	0
  PID  PPID STAT CMD
    1     0 Ss   bash -l
   13     1 R    ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd
State:	S (sleeping)
PPid:	1

head and ps show R because they were running when they looked at themselves. sleep is S: it's waiting for a timer and uses no processor time. In the shell's Ss, the small s marks a session leader, the first process of a terminal's session. The Mac has no /proc folder, though ps -o pid,ppid,stat,command works there too.

sections.h: Starting a program: fork makes a copy, exec swaps the program
sections.html:
A shell has to run ls -l > files.txt: start ls, and send what it prints to a file instead of the screen. The simplest design is one system call (a request to the kernel), say spawn("/usr/bin/ls", args), that creates a process already running ls. It works for plain ls. It breaks for > files.txt, because now ls should write to a file, so spawn needs a setting for where output goes. Then it needs one for input, one for a pipe that feeds one program's output into another, and one for the folder to start in. More follow for the environment variables (named settings a program inherits), the user and the limits. Every new kind of setup becomes one more setting.

Unix took a different route in the 1970s, and Linux kept it. Creating a process is split into two calls, with your own code running in between.

fork() makes a copy of the process that calls it. The child gets a new PID. Everything else starts as a copy of the parent: the code, the memory, the open files and the signal handlers (the fourth section explains signals). Here the family picture breaks, since no child is born with its parent's memories. Both processes come back from the same fork() call. The parent gets the child's PID and the child gets 0, and that's how each one knows which it is. Copying all the memory sounds slow for a big process. In fact the kernel shares the memory, and copies a page, a 4 KB piece of it, only when one side writes to it. Lesson 7, Copy-on-write, mmap and the OOM killer, covers that trick.

execve() replaces the program running in a process. The kernel throws away the old code and memory and loads a new program from disk. The PID stays, and so do the parent and the open files. A successful execve never returns, because the code that called it is gone.

The gap between the two is the point. After fork, the child still runs the shell's code, so it can change things about itself before it becomes ls. A program names its open files with file descriptors, small numbers in which 1 is standard output, where a program's normal output goes. To send output to a file, the child opens the file, then points descriptor 1 at it with dup2. Here is the heart of tinysh.c, a 50-line shell in the labs folder:

pid_t pid = fork();                     // 1. copy this process
if (pid == 0) {                         // child: still tinysh's code
    int fd = open(file, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644);
    dup2(fd, 1);                        // make fd 1 the file
    close(fd);
    execvp(argv[0], argv);              // 2. replace the program
    _exit(127);                         // only reached if exec failed
}
waitpid(pid, &status, 0);               // 3. wait, collect the status

ls knows nothing about files. It writes to descriptor 1, as always, and the shell pointed descriptor 1 at the file before ls started. Pipes, environment variables and limits use the same gap, and no call ever needs a setting for them.

The third call closes the loop. wait() lets the parent sleep until a child ends, then hands it the child's exit status: the number the child passed to exit(), where 0 means success. (On Linux the system call behind it is wait4.) That's where the shell's $? and Java's Process.waitFor() get their number.

You won't find a fork system call in an strace trace on arm64 Linux. (strace, from the last lesson, prints every system call a program makes.) glibc, the C library almost every Linux program uses to talk to the kernel, makes fork() out of clone. It passes the flag SIGCHLD and leaves out CLONE_THREAD, which means "a new process, and tell the parent when it dies". Java's ProcessBuilder, its way of starting other programs, takes another road on Linux, through a small helper program called jspawnhelper. It ends in the same execve and the same wait4. The stepper below follows one command through all three calls. Then we'll look at the moment between the child's end and the parent's wait.

try.title: Run tinysh, then trace it
steps: In the box, build the shell: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/tinysh os/c/l02/tinysh.c. (gcc turns C code into a program you can run.) Read os/c/l02/tinysh.c on your Mac while it builds. It's 50 lines.
Run /tmp/tinysh and type these lines one by one: echo hello from a child, ls /nope, nosuchcmd, ls os > /tmp/listing.txt, cat /tmp/listing.txt, exit.
Now trace it. Run the first command below, type ls os > /tmp/listing.txt and then exit, and print the trace with the second command.

The file is opened in the child, after the clone and before the execve. arm64 has no dup2 system call, so glibc uses dup3. execvp tried a few folders on PATH, the list of folders where a shell looks for programs, before it found /usr/bin/ls. video.title: fork, exec and wait, and the zombie left behind

sections.h: Collecting how it ended: zombies, orphans and wait
sections.html:
A parent often needs to know how its child ended. The shell needs it for $?. A build tool, a program that compiles code in steps, needs it to stop at the first step that failed. But the child may finish long before the parent asks. Where does the answer wait in the meantime?

The simplest design deletes everything when a process ends. Then the exit status is gone before the parent asks. The next simplest keeps the whole process until the parent asks, which wastes its memory and open files, maybe for hours. Linux does something in between. At exit it frees the memory and closes the files at once, and keeps only the small record with the PID and the exit status.

That's the grim word from the first section. A process in that state is a zombie: dead, and still in the table. ps shows it as Z and <defunct>. It uses no processor time and almost no memory. You can't kill it either, because it's already dead. When the parent calls wait, the kernel hands over the status and deletes the record. That last step is called reaping.

The kernel tells the parent about the death with the signal SIGCHLD (the next section explains signals). A shell or a JVM reacts by calling wait. A parent that never waits collects zombies, and each zombie keeps holding a PID.

Now flip the order. If the parent dies first, the child is an orphan. It keeps running, but nobody is left to wait for it. So the kernel gives it a new parent: PID 1, or the nearest ancestor that asked to adopt orphans. (Such an ancestor is called a subreaper, and it asks with the system call prctl.) When the orphan ends, PID 1 has to reap it. On most Linux computers, PID 1 is systemd, the program that starts everything else, and it reaps every orphan it gets.

In a container, PID 1 is whatever program the container starts. (A container is a group of programs that Docker keeps in a box of their own, and the lab box is one.) If that program is a JVM, the program that runs Java code, nobody reaps orphans. The JVM waits for the children it started itself and ignores every other process that ends up under it. Here is a JVM running as PID 1 that started sh -c 'sleep 1 & exit 0'. The small shell started sleep in the background and exited, so sleep became the JVM's orphan. A few seconds later, ps showed:

  PID  PPID STAT CMD
    1     0 Ssl  java /exp/Orphaner.java
   30     1 Z    [sleep] <defunct>

One zombie is harmless. Now picture the café's payments program making a PDF receipt for every payment, by running a small script that leaves a helper running in the background. Each receipt leaves one zombie, and each zombie holds a PID. A container also has a limit on how many PIDs it may use at once. That limit counts threads too, the lines of work inside each program, as the next lesson shows. So in the end, the JVM can't even start a thread. docker run --init, or a tiny program called tini started first, puts a small init program in front of yours. Its only job is to be a good PID 1: it reaps orphans and passes signals on. Next, we'll see what those signals are.

try.title: Make a zombie and an orphan
steps: In the box, build the two programs in os/c/l02/. zombie.c lets its child end at once, and waits 10 seconds before reaping it. orphan.c ends the parent while its child still runs.
Run the commands below. The second ps comes 10 seconds after the first.
Predict the PPID the orphan reports after its parent ends.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/zombie os/c/l02/zombie.c gcc -O2 -o /tmp/orphan os/c/l02/orphan.c /tmp/zombie 10 & sleep 1; ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd sleep 10; ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd /tmp/orphan

try.expect:
parent 57 forked child 59; reaping it in 10 s
  PID  PPID STAT CMD
    1     0 Ss   bash -l
   57     1 S    /tmp/zombie 10
   59    57 Z    [zombie] <defunct>
   60     1 R    ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd
parent reaped 59, exit status 7
  PID  PPID STAT CMD
    1     0 Ss   bash -l
   62     1 R    ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd
child 64: my parent is 63
parent 63: exiting without waiting
child 64: my parent is now 1

For 10 seconds PID 59 is a Z, with its parent's PID next to it. Once the parent calls waitpid, it gets status 7 and the zombie is gone. The orphan's parent changes from 63 to 1, the box's bash shell. bash calls wait for any child it has, so the orphan is reaped when it ends.

sections.h: Stopping a program: SIGTERM asks, SIGKILL doesn't
sections.html:
Back to the opening. Something has to tell the café's payments program to stop: a new version going out, a computer being switched off, a person at a keyboard. How?

The bluntest way is for the kernel to remove the process on request. It always works, and it's a disaster for a program in the middle of its work: half-written files, payments held in memory and never saved, requests cut off halfway. A better way is to send the process a message and let its own code decide what to do. It can finish the work in hand, save what needs saving, then exit. That message is a signal, a small numbered notice the kernel delivers to a process. Some signals come from the kernel itself, such as SIGSEGV for a program that touched memory it doesn't own, or SIGCHLD when a child dies. Others come from another process through the kill system call, which sends any signal, despite its name.

For each signal, a process can choose: do the default action, ignore it, or run a handler, a function the program set up for that signal. For most signals, the default action is to end the process.

Handlers bring their own failure. A buggy or stuck program could catch the stop request and never stop. So Linux keeps two signals that no program can catch, block (hold back for later) or ignore: SIGKILL (9) and SIGSTOP (19). The kernel acts on them without asking the program. That gives you the same two choices as Quit and Force Quit. SIGTERM (15) asks politely, and SIGKILL is the blunt removal for when asking fails.

The JVM sets up handlers for SIGTERM, SIGINT (2, what Ctrl-C sends) and SIGHUP (1). When one arrives, it runs your shutdown hooks, small pieces of code a Java program registers to run on the way out. That's where the payments program would save its three payments, and a logger, the code that notes what a program did, would write out its last lines. Then the JVM exits with status 143. SIGKILL gets none of that:

$ kill -TERM $!; wait $!; echo "exit status: $?"
shutdown hook: flushed 3 pending ledger entries
exit status: 143
$ kill -KILL $!; wait $!; echo "exit status: $?"
exit status: 137

Where do 143 and 137 come from? An exit status is one byte, a number from 0 to 255. When a signal kills a process, wait reports "killed by signal N" instead of an exit status. bash folds that into one number for $?: 128 + N. So 137 is 128 + 9, and 143 is 128 + 15. Java's Process.exitValue() follows the same rule. The JVM's 143 after SIGTERM is a real exit status, though. Its handler caught the signal, ran the hooks, and then exited with the number a shell would have shown anyway.

A polite stop gives a program the chance to finish its work. Ask first.

docker stop uses both tools in order. It sends SIGTERM to the container's PID 1, waits 10 seconds by default, then sends SIGKILL. Kubernetes, a program that big companies use to run many containers across many computers, does the same with a default wait of 30 seconds. So a container that ends with 137 was killed. Either the wait ran out, or the kernel's out-of-memory killer (the OOM killer) ended it for using too much memory, which lesson 7 explains. Even SIGKILL has limits. It does nothing to a zombie, which is already dead, and a process stuck in state D may not die until its disk wait ends.

try.title: SIGTERM against SIGKILL on a JVM
steps: Read os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java. It plays the café's nightly payout job, which pays each shop what it took that day, and which its output calls a settlement batch. It sets up a shutdown hook, then sleeps for a minute as if it were working. The hook only prints a line saying it saved three ledger entries (records of money moved), because it's a stand-in.
In the box, start it in the background, send SIGTERM, and print the exit status. Then do the same with SIGKILL. The sleep 2 gives the JVM time to compile and start the file.
Predict both exit statuses, and whether the hook's line prints each time.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: java os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java & sleep 2; kill -TERM $!; wait $!; echo "exit status: $?" java os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java & sleep 2; kill -KILL $!; wait $!; echo "exit status: $?"

try.expect:
pid 66: settlement batch running
shutdown hook: flushed 3 pending ledger entries
exit status: 143
pid 92: settlement batch running
exit status: 137
bash: line 25:    92 Killed                  java os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java

SIGTERM reached the JVM's handler, the hook ran, and the JVM exited with 143. SIGKILL never reached the program. The kernel ended it, the hook never ran, and bash reported Killed and 137. (Your bash's line number will differ.)

opening:
Picture a café's payments program, which records every card payment, late at night. A new version is ready, so the old one must stop. It still holds three payments in memory that it hasn't saved. Stop it one way, and it saves them, says goodbye and ends with the number 143. Stop it another way, and it vanishes on the spot, with the three payments. All that's left is the number 137.

It's easy to think of stopping a program as one act, like switching off a lamp. Your laptop offers Quit and Force Quit, and from outside both look the same: the window goes away. Only one asks the program first.

In What a kernel does: system calls and user mode, we watched programs ask the kernel for everything, and the kernel kept a record of each. In this lesson, we'll follow a process from birth until its parent learns how it ended, build a tiny shell, leave a zombie behind and stop a Java program both ways. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with the café's payments program on the night of an update, ending with 143 or with 137. 143 means it was asked to stop and saved its work. 137 means the kernel removed it, and nothing it held in memory survived.

In the lab box, run sleep 300 &, then kill -TERM $!; wait $!; echo $?. Do it again with -KILL in place of -TERM, and explain both numbers. On a Mac, the stop button in Activity Monitor offers the same choice, between Quit and Force Quit.

Next, we'll put many lines of work inside one process, and find out what a thread is to the kernel.

compare.title: The same JVM, stopped with SIGTERM and with SIGKILL

a.label: kill -TERM
a.title: lab box
a.html:
$ java os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java &
pid 66: settlement batch running
$ kill -TERM $!; wait $!; echo "exit status: $?"
shutdown hook: flushed 3 pending ledger entries
exit status: 143

b.label: kill -KILL
b.title: lab box
b.html:
$ java os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java &
pid 92: settlement batch running
$ kill -KILL $!; wait $!; echo "exit status: $?"
exit status: 137
bash: line 25:    92 Killed                  java os/src/demo/...

compare.note: SIGTERM is a request. The JVM has a handler for it, runs the shutdown hooks and then exits with 143 (128 + 15) by its own choice. SIGKILL never reaches the program: the kernel ends the process, and wait reports "killed by signal 9", which bash shows as 137. From outside, the two numbers look alike. Only the first one gave your code a chance to finish its work.

worked.title: Why didn't the shutdown hook run on docker stop?

steps.say: A Dockerfile is the recipe Docker uses to build a container: the files to put in it and the command that starts it. Say the payments program's Dockerfile ends with ENTRYPOINT java -jar ledger.jar, where ledger.jar is the packaged Java program. Written this way, called the shell form, Docker runs the command through a shell, /bin/sh -c "...". Reproduce that with the demo and a shell that runs two commands, then look at the processes inside: sh is PID 1, and the JVM is its child.
steps.code: docker run -d --name sfz-os02-stop -v "$PWD":/labs sfz-labbox:1 \ sh -c "echo starting; java /labs/os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java" docker exec sfz-os02-stop ps -o pid,ppid,cmd # PID PPID CMD # 1 0 sh -c echo starting; java /labs/os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java # 7 1 java /labs/os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java

steps.say: Stop it, and give it 3 seconds to finish. The stop takes the full 3 seconds, the hook's line is missing from the log, and the exit status is 137.
steps.code: time docker stop -t 3 sfz-os02-stop # 3.11 s total docker logs sfz-os02-stop # starting # pid 7: settlement batch running docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' sfz-os02-stop # 137 docker rm sfz-os02-stop

steps.say: Why? Docker sent SIGTERM to PID 1, which is sh. The kernel protects a container's PID 1: it delivers a signal from outside only if PID 1 set up a handler for it, and sh has none for SIGTERM. So the signal was dropped, and sh doesn't pass signals on to its children anyway. After 3 seconds Docker sent SIGKILL, which the kernel always delivers. When a container's PID 1 dies, the kernel kills every other process in it, so the JVM died without running its hooks.

The fix: make the JVM itself PID 1. Write the command as a list, called the exec form, ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "ledger.jar"]. Or end a wrapper script with exec java ..., so the shell replaces itself with the JVM. The JVM has a SIGTERM handler, so the signal arrives. Here's the same test with exec:
steps.code: docker run -d --name sfz-os02-stop -v "$PWD":/labs sfz-labbox:1 \ sh -c "echo starting; exec java /labs/os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java" time docker stop -t 3 sfz-os02-stop # 0.11 s total docker logs sfz-os02-stop # starting # pid 1: settlement batch running # shutdown hook: flushed 3 pending ledger entries docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' sfz-os02-stop # 143 docker rm sfz-os02-stop

steps.say: If the JVM starts other programs, add --init too, or put tini first in the entrypoint. The tiny init becomes PID 1, passes SIGTERM on to the JVM and reaps any orphans. You get a clean stop and no zombies.
steps.code: ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/tini", "--", "java", "-jar", "ledger.jar"]

lab.title: Model the kernel's process table
steps: Open ProcessTable.kt. It's a small model of the kernel's table of processes. fork, exec and handle are written for you. Read them first, and note what fork copies and what exec resets.
Run the tests from the labs folder. All ten fail.
Write shellCode, the number a shell would show: one when over the two kinds of ExitStatus.

Write exit through a private helper, terminate(p, status). It marks the process a zombie, gives its children PID 1 as their new parent and, if initReaps is true, removes every zombie whose parent is now PID 1.

Write kill. Handle the cases in the order the KDoc (the comment above the function) gives: a missing PID, a zombie, SIGKILL, a signal with a handler, SIGCHLD, and everything else. The cases that end the process call terminate.
Write waitpid. Find the children of parent (only child, if it isn't -1). No children at all is the error ECHILD. If one is a zombie, remove it and return its PID and status. Otherwise return null.
Run the tests until all ten pass. The last test is this lesson's story of a JVM as PID 1.
hints: check(condition) { "ECHILD: ..." } throws an IllegalStateException with your message, which is what the tests look for.
Re-parent before you reap. A child that was already a zombie becomes init's zombie, and an init that reaps removes it in the same step.
Collect the PIDs to remove into a list first, then remove them. Removing entries from table while you loop over table.values throws ConcurrentModificationException.
Test for SIGKILL before you look at the handlers. A program can't set up a handler for it, so kill shouldn't even look.

drill.title: fork, exec and wait in C, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write C that runs ls -l in a child process and waits for it. Print either its exit status, or the signal that killed it along with the number bash would show. Then say why the child calls _exit and not exit when exec fails.

answer.html: pid_t pid = fork(); if (pid < 0) { perror("fork"); exit(1); } if (pid == 0) { // child execlp("ls", "ls", "-l", (char *)NULL); perror("exec"); // only runs if exec failed _exit(127); // skip the stdio buffers and atexit } // handlers copied from the parent int status; waitpid(pid, &status, 0); // parent: sleep until the child ends if (WIFEXITED(status)) printf("exit code %d\n", WEXITSTATUS(status)); else if (WIFSIGNALED(status)) printf("signal %d, bash shows %d\n", WTERMSIG(status), 128 + WTERMSIG(status));

recap: A process is a running program plus the kernel's record of it: PID, parent, state, memory, open files and signal settings. /proc/<pid>/status shows the record.
fork copies the caller, execve replaces the program but keeps the PID and the open files, and wait collects the exit status. The gap between fork and exec is where a shell sends output to a file.
A dead process stays a zombie (Z) until its parent waits. An orphan gets PID 1 as its new parent, and PID 1 must reap it.
SIGTERM can be caught, so the JVM runs its shutdown hooks and exits with 143. SIGKILL can't, so nothing runs and the shell shows 137, which is 128 + 9.
In a container your program may be PID 1. A JVM there doesn't reap orphans, and a shell there drops SIGTERM. Start the JVM with the exec form, and add --init when it starts other programs.
The limit: every process in this lesson does one thing at a time. A program that must wait on many things at once needs several lines of work inside it, and that's the next lesson.

explain.prompt: A friend runs the café's payments program in a container. On their laptop it stops cleanly with Ctrl-C, but on every update in the container it ends with exit status 137. Explain what's going on, and what you'd check.
explain.answer: 137 means the process was killed by signal 9, SIGKILL, because shells and container tools report 128 plus the signal number. SIGKILL can't be caught, so the JVM's shutdown hooks never ran. On the laptop, Ctrl-C sends SIGINT, which the JVM catches, and it runs the hooks. On an update, the container tool first sends SIGTERM to PID 1, and sends SIGKILL only after a wait, 10 seconds for docker stop. So either SIGTERM never reached the JVM, or stopping took longer than the wait. I'd check how the container starts first. If PID 1 is a shell that doesn't exec java, the kernel drops SIGTERM, because the shell has no handler for it, and the JVM only ever sees SIGKILL. Then I'd check whether the hooks finish within the wait. If both are fine, I'd look for the kernel's OOM killer, which also leaves 137.

deeper.html:
ProcessBuilder.start(), Java's way of starting another program, doesn't call fork on Linux. Copying a JVM with a big heap and dozens of threads, even with copy-on-write, is wasted work when the child is about to exec anyway. Since JDK 13 (JDK-8213192), the default on Linux is posix_spawn, a C library function that starts a program in one step. The JDK, the JVM plus its tools, runs a small helper, jspawnhelper, which then execs your command. Here's a trace of new ProcessBuilder("ls", "/labs").start() on JDK 25 in the lab box (trimmed):

39    clone3({flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_VFORK|CLONE_CLEAR_SIGHAND, exit_signal=SIGCHLD, ...}, 88) = -1 ENOSYS (Function not implemented)
39    clone(child_stack=0xffffb85ed000, flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_VFORK|SIGCHLD <unfinished ...>
59    execve("/opt/java/openjdk/lib/jspawnhelper", ["/opt/java/openjdk/lib/jspawnhelp"..., "25.0.5+8-LTS", "10:11:13"], ...) = 0
59    execve("/usr/bin/ls", ["ls", "/labs"], ...) = 0
39    --- SIGCHLD {si_signo=SIGCHLD, si_code=CLD_EXITED, si_pid=59, si_uid=0, si_status=0, si_utime=0, si_stime=0} ---
60    wait4(59, [{WIFEXITED(s) && WEXITSTATUS(s) == 0}], 0, NULL) = 59

CLONE_VM|CLONE_VFORK is the vfork pattern. The child shares the parent's memory instead of copying it, and the parent's thread pauses until the child calls execve. Nothing is copied, so it costs the same for a 100 MB JVM as for a 30 GB one. (The clone3 and ENOSYS pair is Docker's seccomp filter again, from What a kernel does.) The wait4 comes from thread 60, the JDK's "process reaper" thread. It waits for each child the JVM started, and completes Process.onExit(), an object that holds the result once the child ends. That thread is the reason a JVM reaps its own children and nobody else's.

Two more details are worth knowing. /proc/<pid>/status has bit masks, one bit per signal, for the signals a process blocks, ignores and catches (SigBlk, SigIgn, SigCgt). For the demo JVM, SigCgt decodes to SIGHUP, SIGQUIT, SIGILL, SIGBUS, SIGFPE, SIGSEGV, SIGUSR2, SIGPIPE, SIGTERM and SIGXFSZ, plus two real-time signals. The JVM catches SIGSEGV, the bad-memory signal, on purpose: it's part of how it checks for null references and pauses its threads. SIGQUIT (kill -3) makes it print a thread dump, a list of what every thread is doing, which the next lesson uses. And SIGINT was missing from that mask. bash starts background jobs with SIGINT ignored, and the JVM leaves an ignored signal ignored. A kill -INT to that background JVM did nothing at all.
